# How the restart routine can go wrong

Written before `router.sh` and `task.sh`, and updated with each review. Each line is a failure and the defence the code has for it.
"Router" is the `router` job in `fleet.yml`, "task job" is the agent's `task` job, "outcome job" is the `outcome` job that judges it, and "check" is `task.sh check`.

A start is a run with outcome `progress`, `failed` or `done`. `paused` and `cancelled` aren't starts. A run is recorded `cancelled` only when its job was cancelled and the issue has `fleet:stop`; any other cancelled job (a manual cancel, or GitHub's own job timeout, which may also report cancelled) is recorded `progress`, so it counts.

| # | Failure | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Double start: two router runs (cron and a label event) dispatch the same task at once | Rounds share the concurrency group `fleet-router-round` and run one at a time. Each dispatch is a run named `task #<n>`, and a queued, pending or in-progress run with that name means "running". A round doesn't end until each run it started is in the run list (29). If a second dispatch still slips through, the task job's own group `fleet-task-<n>` (no cancel) makes it wait, and its check finds the PR state the first one left. One writer per task at any time. Cost: a pending run that a newer one replaces in that group ends cancelled with no `fleet:stop`, so it's recorded `progress` and counts as a start. It takes a double dispatch, so at worst one extra start. |
| 2 | Restart of a stopped task | `fleet:stop` cancels every active `task #<n>` run. Each stop event has its own concurrency group `fleet-router-stop-<n>`, so a burst of stop labels is never dropped as a superseded pending run. The router skips any issue with `fleet:stop` and cancels whatever it still has running, and check stops the task job cleanly if the label is there when it starts. "Stop all" (the `stop_all` dispatch input) labels every open task and cancels every task run, in its own group. |
| 3 | Restart of a task waiting to land | A ready PR in the merge queue, or with auto-merge on and checks pending or passing, is "waiting". Merge queue state comes from GraphQL `isInMergeQueue`. |
| 4 | A ready PR that can't land is never repaired | A ready PR whose checks failed or errored is unfinished whatever auto-merge says. A ready PR that isn't in the queue and conflicts with its base (GraphQL `mergeable` is `CONFLICTING`) is unfinished whatever auto-merge and checks say: a sibling task merging first makes this the normal case, and a conflicting PR gets no new ci run. A ready PR with auto-merge off and not queued is unfinished. Drafts, closed-only PRs and no PR are unfinished. Open question for the live proof: does GitHub turn auto-merge off when the queue drops a PR? If it doesn't, the checks passed and the PR doesn't conflict, the task waits on a PR that will never land. |
| 5 | Forged marker comment | Only comments whose author is `github-actions[bot]` (type `Bot`) count, and the marker must be the comment's whole first line. Markers are posted only by the outcome job. The task job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` has no `issues: write`, and the agent's Claude app token is cut to `issues: read` (`additional_permissions`), so the agent can't post, edit or delete a marker or remove `fleet:stop` or `fleet:failed` with the tokens it's given (see 21 for the ones it might take). `ci.yml` has `contents: read` only. |
| 6 | Issue written or edited by someone else | Only issues whose author is `FLEET_OWNER` start, compared without letter case. An issue with no author can't start. A missing `FLEET_OWNER` fails the job instead of trusting everyone. Edits by others need write access, and the brief is read fresh at each start. |
| 7 | Cap never reached | Starts are counted from markers: at most `FLEET_MAX_STARTS` (default 6) starts, and two `failed` starts in a row is also a cap. `done` counts, so a PR the queue keeps dropping can't loop forever, and so does a cancelled job without `fleet:stop`, so a job that keeps hanging or being cancelled can't either. The outcome job runs on its own runner after every task run, including a lost runner, a job timeout and a cancel: a task job that died without outputs is recorded as `failed`. It runs the cap check after every marker, `done` included, and the run that hits the cap adds the label and the Telegram alert. One exception: when the cap is reached and the task's PR is merged, queued or set to merge, the outcome job doesn't label or alert, because the PR may still land. If it drops, the router labels the task on a later round and its `router-alert` job tells Telegram. The router alerts for every task it labels. A run cancelled by hand without `fleet:stop` is recorded `progress`, so its end starts a round (30) and the task restarts within seconds, using a start: to stop a task, add `fleet:stop` first. Gap: a run cancelled with "force cancel" may skip the outcome job and leave no marker. |
| 8 | Cron late or skipped | GitHub's docs: "The `schedule` event can be delayed during periods of high loads of GitHub Actions workflow runs. High load times include the start of every hour. If the load is sufficiently high enough, some queued jobs may be dropped." They advise: "To decrease the chance of delay, schedule your workflow to run at a different time of the hour." So the cron asks for minutes 7 and 37, not 0 and 30. That lowers the chance of delay. It doesn't promise a round every 30 minutes: with the cron at 0 and 30, no scheduled round ran in the first hour after the merge. Also from the docs: "In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days." Label events and the end of a task run that counted as a start also start the router (30), and nothing depends on the cron being on time: a late or dropped round just starts work later. Some restarts do depend on it firing at all, and it never has on this repo (34). A run end speeds up only the restart of that same task. A PR that merges into a fleet branch starts its own round (37), which closes its issue and can open the final PR. |
| 9 | Dispatch or another change fails | Each failed `gh` change is logged and counted, the router carries on with the other tasks and then exits non-zero so the run shows red. The next round tries again. |
| 10 | One issue's state can't be read | Each issue is decided in its own subshell. An API error or an unreadable value skips that issue with a warning, and the round carries on. A `retry_after` that can't be read is treated as empty: its seat is blocked for one hour after the marker (see 15). |
| 11 | API pagination past 30 or 100 items | Issues, comments, blockers and branches use `gh api --paginate --slurp` with `per_page=100`. Runs use the same, one request per status, and GitHub returns up to 1,000 runs per status. PRs are looked up per head branch and base branch, 100 at a time. |
| 12 | Issue with no `Base:` line, or a base branch that doesn't exist | The task job fails before the checkout, and the outcome job records `failed`. Two in a row add `fleet:failed`. |
| 13 | Deleted task branch | GitHub closes the PR. The task job finds no `task/<n>` on the remote and creates it again from the base, and the agent opens a new PR. |
| 14 | Closed, unmerged PR | Not "waiting", not "done", so the task is unfinished and the agent opens a new PR. To stop a task, use `fleet:stop`, not closing the PR. |
| 15 | Usage limit loops | A run that hits a seat limit records `paused` with the reset time when the SDK gives one. The matcher reads only the newest `rate_limit_event`, and counts it only when it's `rejected` and overage isn't carrying the session. A `retry_after` more than 8 days ahead is recorded as 8 days. A paused marker blocks only its own seat for that task: until its `retry_after`, or for one hour after the marker when `retry_after` is empty or unreadable. The seat rotation starts at the issue number mod 3 and moves on by one for every earlier marker that isn't `cancelled`, a pause included, and the router takes the first seat in that order that isn't blocked. With all three blocked, the task is skipped until the first one frees. Paused runs aren't starts and there is no cap on pauses, so a task can wait on limits for as long as they last. Cost: when every seat is out of usage and the SDK gives no reset time, each task costs up to three short jobs an hour (one per seat), for as long as the limits last. An execution file that can't be parsed is recorded as not paused, with only a warning in the log (`task.sh usage`). A run that really hit a usage limit is then recorded as a start (`progress`, or `failed` when the agent step failed and wasn't cut off): its seat isn't blocked for the task, the start is used, and two such failures in a row add `fleet:failed`. |
| 16 | Job killed at the 6 hour limit | The agent step stops at 55 minutes, well before it, because the agent's GitHub access ends after an hour (33). The job stops at 80, so the steps before the agent and the checkpoint after it get their time. The outcome job runs on its own runner whatever happens to the task job. A step cut off at its timeout fails, and the outcome job records `progress`, not `failed`: it counts a run as cut off when at least `AGENT_TIMEOUT_MINUTES` (55, the same number) passed since the job started (`ran_to_timeout` in `lib.sh`, tested in `classify-test.sh`, which also checks that `fleet.yml` uses 55 in all three places: the step's timeout, `AGENT_TIMEOUT_MINUTES` and the stop time the agent is told). The agent step starts seconds after the job, so a cut-off step always counts. GitHub's docs don't say how a step that hits its `timeout-minutes` is reported. The runner's source does: it records the step as failed ("The action '...' has timed out after N minutes." in `StepsRunner.cs`), then applies `continue-on-error`, so the step's outcome is `failure` and the job goes on to the checkpoint. Not seen live yet. Cost: some real failures are recorded `progress`, not `failed`. The outcome job reads its clock after the checkpoint and after it waits for a runner, so a step that fails on its own near the end counts as cut off once 55 minutes have passed by then. With a few minutes of queue for the outcome job, that reaches back to failures at minute 45 or so. Such a run doesn't count toward "two failed runs in a row", but it is still a start, so the start cap (`FLEET_MAX_STARTS`, 6) bounds it: a task that keeps failing near the end uses all its starts before `fleet:failed`, instead of stopping after two. |
| 17 | Work lost when a run dies | The checkpoint commits and pushes what's left in the tree with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, with git hooks off. A push with `GITHUB_TOKEN` gets no ci without a person (28), so it runs only when the task has no PR or a draft one, never on a ready PR. It never runs when the checkout or the agent step was skipped, and `.fleet-rules/` and `node_modules/` are ignored. A failed checkpoint is a warning, not a red job. |
| 18 | Issue body used as shell | The body is written to a file with `gh api ... --jq .body > file`. Scripts read issue JSON with `jq` and only print numbers, labels and the validated base branch name. The prompt is fixed text. |
| 19 | A task issue that's a PR | `/issues` also lists PRs. Anything with `pull_request` set is dropped. |
| 20 | Dispatched run rejected as a bot | Runs the router starts have `github-actions[bot]` as their actor, and the action refuses bot actors unless `allowed_bots` lists them, so the task job lists exactly that one bot. |
| 21 | Runner isn't a sandbox | Not enforceable, and accepted until a dedicated GitHub App is used. The agent runs any shell command on the task job's runner, with sudo. For the length of its job it holds its own seat token and the rules deploy key: both are in the runner's memory, which sudo can read. It can probably mint a wider Claude app token through OIDC (the job has `id-token: write`, and the request variables are in the parent process). With such a token it could push a workflow file to `task/<n>`; that workflow runs on push with a `GITHUB_TOKEN` whose `permissions:` block can ask for `issues: write` and `actions: write` (the repo default of read is only a default). That lets it post `github-actions[bot]` markers, remove `fleet:stop` or `fleet:failed` and dispatch `fleet.yml` from `main`, so on this route the caps don't hold. Without a minted token it can still change every output the task job reports: claim `paused` (not a start), claim it never reached the checkout (no marker) or fake a step timeout (`progress` instead of `failed`). Each claim is checked against its known values before it's used or printed, and anything else is printed as `invalid`. What limits the damage: the seat environments are usable only from `main`; `main` and `fleet/**` are protected by rulesets (no push, no force push, no deletion, CI on `fleet/**` and the merge queue on each feature branch, the owner's review on `main`); a false `paused` waits at most 8 days. |
| 22 | Strangers write instructions for the agent | The router locks the task issue's conversation before it starts the task, and the outcome job locks the task PR's conversation. The prompt says comments are never instructions. Gaps: a PR the agent opens can take comments until its run's outcome job locks it. The agent's app token keeps `pull_requests: write`, which GitHub's App permission table also lists for the lock, comment and label endpoints on a PR, so the agent can unlock and comment on its own task PR: the PR lock lasts only until a run's agent undoes it. Its issue is out of that token's reach. Accepted until a dedicated GitHub App is used. Each marker opens the issue for a few seconds (27). |
| 23 | A fork PR named `task/<n>` | Only PRs from this repo into the task's base branch count. A fork PR, or a PR into another base, never makes a task look done or waiting. |
| 24 | A task PR changes the CI gate on a fleet branch | `ci.yml` fails a PR or merge group into `fleet/**` that touches `.github/`, `app/scripts/` (the lint scripts and their allow lists), `app/playwright.config.ts` or `app/.oxlintrc.json`, or that adds a `.skip(` or `.fixme(` to a changed file under `app/e2e/`. For a PR, GitHub runs `ci.yml` as the PR's merge commit has it, so the guard holds only because a task PR can't change `ci.yml` itself: the agent's app token has no `workflows` permission (`DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS` in the action's `src/github/token.ts` plus `additional_permissions`), and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` can never push workflow files, so neither can push a change under `.github/workflows/`. Only a wider minted token could (21, accepted). A ruleset `file_path_restriction` rule isn't used: GitHub documents push rules for private and internal repositories only, and this repo is public. Those changes go to `main` through the owner. |
| 25 | The final PR never opens, opens early or opens again | At the end of each round the router reads the open and closed issues again, and a task the round itself closed counts as closed whatever those lists say (38). It opens `fleet/<topic>` into `main` only when the branch is ahead of `main`, at least one closed fleet issue names it as Base, no open fleet issue names it (stopped and failed tasks count as open), no PR into `main` is open, and no closed, unmerged PR into `main` has the branch's current head: a final PR the owner closed isn't reopened until the branch moves on. A PR opened with `GITHUB_TOKEN` gets only a ci run that waits for approval (28), so the router then dispatches `ci.yml` on the branch, and its `ci` check lands on the head commit. Telegram hears "ready for review". |
| 26 | A failed task restarted by removing `fleet:failed` | It isn't: its markers still count, so the next round labels it again. Close the issue and open a new one to retry. |
| 27 | GitHub refuses a bot's comment on a locked issue | Reported for `github-actions[bot]` and App tokens (403 "issue is locked"), and GitHub's docs don't settle it. Every comment the fleet posts goes through one helper (`comment_on` in `lib.sh`): if the conversation is locked it unlocks it, posts, then locks it again, and locks it again even when the post fails. A failed lock-again is a warning, never fatal. Cost: the issue is open to comments for the few seconds between the unlock and the lock, once per marker and once when the router closes a done task. Nothing posted then reaches the agent: the brief is the issue body, and comments are never instructions. A failed marker post fails the outcome job, loudly. |
| 28 | A finished task waits on a PR head that never got ci | GitHub's docs: "When a pull request is created or updated by a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `pull_request` events with the `opened`, `synchronize`, or `reopened` activity types create workflow runs that require approval." So a checkpoint push to a draft task PR, and the final PR the router opens, each get a ci run that waits for a person. Neither relies on that run. The next task run's `gh pr ready` uses the app token, whose events start workflows as usual: `ci.yml` listens to `ready_for_review` as well as opened, synchronize and reopened. The router dispatches `ci.yml` on the final PR's branch (25). Seen live: run 44218947121, the `pull_request` run for the checkpoint push to draft PR #21 (task #16, head `6ee9c1d`, by `github-actions[bot]`), ended `action_required` with no jobs. Its check suite has no check runs, and that head has no check run and no status at all, so no `ci` check, pending or failing. So a task whose last commit came from the checkpoint has a head without `ci` until its next run: that run's own push, or its `gh pr ready` on that same head (the app token, so `ready_for_review` starts `ci`), gives the head its `ci`. With the 55 minute stop (33) more runs end on a checkpoint push, so this is the normal case. Not seen live yet: whether such a run left on a head blocks auto-merge or the queue once the PR is ready. |
| 29 | A round misses the run the round before it started, and starts the task again | Seen live: task #6 got runs 44207376583 and 44207411001 from rounds 44207318636 and 44207343001, and task #17 got 44208417117 and 44208485041 from rounds 44208349309 and 44208359628. The second round's run list left out a run that had been in progress for 12 and for 21 seconds, while it listed runs dispatched just before and after it. That list filters by status, which GitHub's REST docs count as a search. For #17 it cost a start: both runs failed, and two failed runs in a row added `fleet:failed` one round early. Now the router dispatches through the REST endpoint with `return_run_details` sent as a JSON boolean (`-F`). Without it the endpoint answers `204 No Content` with no body (GitHub changelog, 2026-02-19: "If you do not pass in this parameter, it will continue to return the current `204 No Content` status code"), as seen on this repo. With it, `200` and the new run's id (`workflow_run_id`). A dispatch that still returns no numeric id is an error naming the task, and the round ends red. The round doesn't end until each run it started is in that same list or has finished. It checks up to 13 times with a 5 second sleep between checks: 60 seconds of sleep plus the time the reads take, so the wait runs longer than a minute. A run that never shows fails the round with an error naming the task and the number of checks. A run list that fails during the wait is a warning naming the tasks, and the next check tries again. Nothing in the dispatch loop exits the round, so the runs already started are always waited for, and `failed_tasks` and `final_prs` are always written. Rounds run one at a time, so the next round sees the run. The stop rounds (`stop-all`, `stop-<n>`) only label and cancel, and never dispatch. The wait is tested against fixtures, and the live dispatch and wait against a stub `gh` (`dispatch-test.sh`). The lag itself shows only live. |
| 30 | A finished task waits for its restart, or the rounds that task runs start never stop | A task run's last job, `next-round`, dispatches `fleet.yml` with `after_run` set to its own run id, and that round runs in the usual group `fleet-router-round`. A dispatch with `GITHUB_TOKEN` is one of the events GitHub documents as always creating a run, so no other token is needed. The run is still in progress while the round reads the run list, so the router leaves out exactly that run id: without that, the task would look running and be skipped. `workflow_run` wasn't taken: it would fire when any `fleet` run completes, rounds included, and GitHub doesn't document a workflow triggering on its own runs. Order: the outcome job sets `next_round` only after the marker is posted and the caps are applied, so the round never decides on stale markers. No loop: only a task run has the job, and only after a start (`progress`, `failed` or `done`), so every link in the chain counts toward the start cap. `paused`, `cancelled` and a run that recorded nothing start no round. `paused` isn't a start and its `retry_after` has no lower bound, so a false claim would otherwise restart the task at once, without end. A task paused on a usage limit waits for the next round from another trigger, as it did before. The caps hold: two failed runs in a row still add `fleet:failed`, and a paused seat is still skipped. Cost, accepted: a task that can never finish uses all its starts (`FLEET_MAX_STARTS`) in minutes, and a run cancelled by hand without `fleet:stop` restarts within seconds (7). What gets faster is the restart of the task whose run ended. A task blocked by another doesn't: its blocker clears when the blocking issue closes, which a round does only after that task's PR has merged, so the round the finishing run starts still sees it blocked. It starts on the round its blocker's merge starts (37) only if its number is higher than its blocker's: the round works oldest first, so a blocked task with a lower number is read before its blocker closes and waits for a later trigger (34). Gap: the run list lags (29), so any round can count a run that has just ended as still running, and that task then waits for the next trigger, at worst the cron, which has never fired on this repo (34). A new pending round replaces an older one in the group, but that costs little: the round that runs reads every issue, and the earlier run has normally finished by then. Merges now put more plain rounds into `fleet-router-round` (37), so a `merged-round` dispatch replaces a pending `after_run=<id>` round from `next-round` more often than before. If the run list still lags (29), the plain round that runs can count that ending run as still running and skip its restart until a later trigger (34). The job has `actions: write` only and no environment or secret. Anyone who can dispatch `fleet.yml` can set `after_run`, which only makes a round skip one run: the same people can already dispatch a task. |
| 31 | Stop all, or `fleet:stop`, races a round | The stop rounds run in their own groups, beside a round (2), and a round can now start whenever a task run ends. A round reads the issue again right before each dispatch, and doesn't start a task that has `fleet:stop` by then (`dispatch-test.sh`). Left open: a label added between that read and the dispatch. Then the task job's check stops the run cleanly if the label is there when the job starts. If the run passed its check first, the stop round cancels it only if its run list shows it, and that list lags (29). A stop round whose run list can't be read, or whose cancel fails, ends red with an error naming the task (`dispatch-test.sh`). A run that slips past all of this keeps working until a later round cancels whatever a stopped task has running. That's the next round from any trigger, and at worst the cron, which has never fired on this repo (34). A round held back below the budget floor cancels nothing (32), so while either budget is under the floor that can take until the budget resets, up to an hour. |
| 32 | The fleet runs out of API calls | GitHub's docs: "The rate limit for `GITHUB_TOKEN` is 1,000 requests per hour per repository." Every job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` in this repo shares it. The agent uses the Claude app's token, not this one. Cut: the active runs are read with one REST request per status (5), not `gh run list` (2 each), and a cancel or a ci start is one request, not `gh run cancel` (3) or `gh workflow run` (2). Counted from the code, in REST requests: a round with nothing to start costs 6 (issues and runs), plus 2 per open task it reads in full (1 if blocked, 0 if it's running, merged, stopped, failed or set to merge), plus 1 for the branch list, 2 more when a `fleet/` branch exists and 1 per branch (5 for a branch whose final PR opens). A start adds 3 (2 once the issue is locked), and the wait adds 5 per poll plus 1 per run not yet listed. A task run's own jobs make 12 or 13 (task job 7, outcome 4 or 5, next-round 1), checkouts not counted. So a run end and the round it starts cost about 30, where they cost 50 to 80 before. A read-only dry run on this repo with 5 open tasks and nothing to start made 11 REST requests, and the budget fell by exactly 11. GraphQL is a second budget: "For `GITHUB_TOKEN` in GitHub Actions workflows: 1,000 points per hour per repository." and "The REST API also has a separate primary rate limit." The PR lookups, the marker comment, labels, closes and `gh pr create` use it, at least 1 point a call. A round reads the PRs of every open, owner-written fleet issue with a Base line, running, stopped or failed ones included, so with many of those GraphQL can run out before REST. Logged: each round prints `fleet budget: REST <left>/<limit> resets <time> UTC, GraphQL <left>/<limit> resets <time> UTC` at its start and end, and each outcome job at its end. `GET /rate_limit` gives both and doesn't count ("Accessing this endpoint does not count against your REST API rate limit."). A figure that can't be read (missing, or not a whole number) is printed `unreadable` on a warning line. Guard: a round that starts with less than `FLEET_BUDGET_FLOOR` (default 200) left in either budget warns with the numbers and ends green, which leaves room for the outcome jobs' markers. Such a held round does nothing else either: it starts no task, opens no final PR, closes no done issue, labels no capped task (so that alert waits too) and doesn't cancel what a stopped task still has running (31). Nothing is lost: each of those is read again from GitHub by the next round that isn't held back, until the budget resets, up to an hour. A held round only warns. It sets no alert, so a fleet sitting below the floor shows only in the log. `fleet:stop` and stop all run first, whatever the budget and whatever the floor's value. A figure that can't be read doesn't hold a round back. A floor of 0 turns the guard off. Any other value fails every round but the stop rounds, red: the floor must be digits only, 0 or 1 to 9999999999 with no leading zero, so `08`, `+5` and `5.0` fail too. Such a round reads the budget first and then nothing else. A label event that isn't a stop ends green before the check. Not measured: the live cost of a real wave, and whether 200 is enough. A round that starts above the floor can still spend past it (about 5 per start and 5 per poll). |
| 33 | The agent loses its GitHub access after an hour | Seen live: task #16, run 44208892119, ran 77 minutes. The action minted its app token at 00:34:33Z, 13 seconds after the job started. The agent updated its PR until minute 59, then no more, and the action's own cleanup got `401 Bad credentials` at 01:51:11Z. Its last commit was pushed by the checkpoint with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and the run was recorded `progress`. GitHub's docs: "The installation access token will expire after 1 hour." The pinned action (`src/github/token.ts`, `setupGitHubToken`) exchanges the job's OIDC token for one app token once, at the start of its step, and never renews it. After the hour the agent can still work, but it can't push, edit its PR, mark it ready or turn on auto-merge. What stops it: the agent step stops at 55 minutes (16). A step before it works out that stop time in UTC, and the prompt gives it to the agent: by 10 minutes before it, the agent commits, pushes, updates the Progress section and ends its turn. The checkpoint pushes anything left. The run is recorded `progress`, its end starts a round (30), and the next run gets a fresh token and carries on from the Progress section. Cost: every restart is a start, so with `FLEET_MAX_STARTS` at 6 one task gets at most about five and a half hours of agent time (6 times 55 minutes). A bigger task needs a higher cap, or a token that lasts longer (the action takes one as `github_token`). |
| 34 | Deferred restarts wait for a schedule that has never fired | These all wait for the next round from another trigger: a task paused on a usage limit (30), a round held back below the budget floor (32), a task the lagging run list showed as still running (29, 30), a failed `next-round` dispatch, a stopped task's run that slipped past its stop round (31), a failed `merged-round` dispatch, a merge into a fleet branch cut before `merged-round` existed, and a blocked task the round of its blocker's merge read before closing the blocker (37). When no other task is running and nobody adds a label, that trigger is the cron. Seen live: no `schedule` run has ever been created on this repo (`GET /actions/runs?event=schedule` gave `total_count` 0 at 02:22 UTC on 18 November 2026, after the 00:30, 01:00, 01:30 and 02:00 slots of the cron on `main`). Those rounds all end green, and nothing alerts. So a lone paused task can stall with no sign but its marker. Not relied on until a scheduled round has been seen live on this repo. Until then, a stalled task restarts when a label is added or another task's run ends, or by hand: run the `fleet` workflow with no inputs. |
| 35 | A run list that can't be read whole | Found in review: `api_active_runs` passed the whole list of active runs to `jq` as one argument. A live run object is about 13 KB, and Linux refuses a program argument of 131072 bytes or more, so with 9 or more active runs `jq` couldn't start. The function always runs inside `$(...)`, where bash turns errexit off, so it printed nothing and exited 0. The stop rounds then cancelled nothing and ended green, and a round started tasks that were running and ignored the job cap. Now each page keeps only the id, title and status, the pages are joined on stdin, and each step in the function ends the round with a message naming it. `dispatch-test.sh` reads 12 runs of 13 KB through a `jq` that refuses a big argument as Linux does, so it fails on a Mac too: `fleet:stop` cancels its run, stop all cancels all 12, and a round counts 12 and skips the running task. ## Known and accepted

- The rulesets on `main` and `fleet/**` (and each `fleet/<topic> queue`) let the repo admin role bypass them. It's there for the owner only: to create feature branches (`new-feature.sh`), and to merge workflow fixes the owner's own agents open, since an author can't approve their own PR. The bots have no bypass.
- The rules deploy key reads the whole private `agents-config` repo, not just the files copied to `~/.claude`. A separate rules-only repo with its own key would limit that. Not taken this round.
- The Claude app may hold the Workflows permission. A dedicated GitHub App without it, passed as `github_token`, would close the OIDC route in 21. Not taken this round.
- The Workflows permission matters because a minted token could push a workflow to `task/<n>`. That workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can ask for `issues: write` and `actions: write`, which is enough to forge markers, remove `fleet:stop` or `fleet:failed` and dispatch `fleet.yml` (21). The rulesets still stop it from reaching `main` or `fleet/**`. Accepted until the dedicated App is used.
- The agent can unlock and comment on its own task PR with its app token (22). Accepted until the dedicated App is used.
